newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Airports earn most from non-flights operations.
newsitem.headline: Airports earn most from non-flights operations.

text.p: Airports in richer countries earn more from services like duty-free shops and parking than from fees paid by airlines such as landing charges, the world airports body ACI reported on Monday.

But in the developing countries of Asia, Africa and Latin America, where passenger flows are much smaller, aeronautical revenues can account for up to 64 per cent of airports' income, said ACI, the Airports Council International.

The findings were included in the results of a survey taken in 1996 by the 475-member ACI, to which members operating 246 airports handling 40 per cent of the world's annual flow of some 2.5 billion passengers replied.

The survey also found that the average number of people employed at respondent airports by the airport operators was 290, while an average of 3,200 more were employed by other entities at each airport.
"This adds considerable weight to the contention that airports are centres of employment and generators of economic growth," ACI said.

At the same time, the survey pointed to a vast diversity in the size of airports and their structure. At several of the largest, over 50,000 people were employed while the smallest provided jobs for only around 25.

Overall revenues reported by 222 of the respondent airports for 1995 were $9.4 billion, of which $4.8 billion or 53 per cent came from aeronautical sources and $4.6 billion or 47 per cent from non-aeronautical sources.

A total of 24 airports did not provide a breakdown, giving only a single figure for revenues. But with their income taken into account, total revenues for all airports who replied was $11.4 billion, or some $46 billion per airport.
In Europe, where the duty-free shopping business is well-developed, non-aeronautical revenues reached 55.9 per cent of airport incomes.
In North America, it was 51.4 per cent and in the Pacific region -- which in ACI terminology covers Japan, Australasia, South Korea and most of South-East Asia, exactly 50 per cent.
But in Asia, for ACI the Indian sub-continent and the Middle East, airline fees accounted for 64 per cent, in Africa 60 per cent, and in Latin America and the Caribbean 58.4 per cent.

ACI said small passenger flows through the airports of these regions "limits their potential to generate landside revenues from retail concessions, parking and other uses or airport property, such as hotels and conference centres."

The survey also highlighted strong differences in airport employment structure not only between the developed and developing countries but also between North America on the Pacific on one hand and Europe on the other.
Globally, the ratio of people directly employed by airport operators to all those employed on the airport premises was about 1 to 10, the ACI found.

But in North America, where contracting out of ground services has made most advances, and in the Pacific, the average was 1 to 20, whereas in Europe -- where many airports use their own employees to provide ground services -- it was 1 to 8.

ACI cited one European airport, which it did not identify, reported over 10,000 payroll employees engaged in ground- handling activities, while a similar large hub in the United States directly employed only 19 out of 9,000 people working on its premises.
In Asia, the ratio was 1 to 3, largely due to the large percentage of civil servants employed at airports.
